title: Trademark Protection in India for a Foreign Company: Madrid Protocol Designation or Direct National Filing
subtitle: The choice a foreign brand owner makes before its first Indian filing decides how exposed the registration stays to a fight happening in an entirely different country.
meta_description: Madrid Protocol designation versus direct filing for a foreign company's Indian trademark: central attack, timelines, Section 154 priority and renewal.
author: Bhaskar Subramanian
standfirst: A foreign company planning its first Indian trademark filing is usually offered two routes by its agent almost in the same breath: designate India under the Madrid Protocol using the mark already registered at home, or file directly before the Indian Trade Marks Registry as a fresh national application. The two routes lead to the same register, but they do not carry the same risk, the same timeline, or the same flexibility once the filing is made, and the choice is harder to reverse than the marketing team planning the India launch usually expects.
key_points: India has been a member of the Madrid Protocol since the treaty entered into force for it on 8 July 2013, following accession deposited with WIPO on 8 April 2013, making India the 90th member of the Madrid Union.

A Madrid designation of India is examined under Chapter IVA of the Trade Marks Act, 1999, inserted by the Trade Marks (Amendment) Act, 2010, and India has declared an 18-month period for notifying a provisional refusal rather than the shorter default period.

A Madrid-based registration remains dependent on the foreign applicant's home basic mark for five years from the international registration date, so a successful challenge to the home mark within that window can take the Indian designation down with it.

A foreign applicant can instead file directly before the Indian Registry, which needs an Indian address for service, a locally executed or apostilled power of attorney on Form TM-48, and generally more flexibility in how the specification of goods or services is worded for Indian practice.
A direct filing can claim a priority date under Section 154 from an earlier application in a convention country if the Indian filing is made within six months of that earlier filing.

Opposition in India has to be filed within four months of advertisement under Section 21(1), a period the current wording does not allow to be extended, so docketing this date correctly matters more in India than in jurisdictions with a more forgiving opposition window.

A registration lasts ten years and can be renewed indefinitely, but the renewal, late-renewal and restoration windows under Section 25 run on their own strict clock, and a mark struck off for more than a year generally has to be refiled from scratch with no priority carried over.

sections.heading: Two Ways Into the Indian Register
paragraphs: A foreign company's brand almost always exists somewhere else first, registered at home or in whichever jurisdiction the company first traded under it, before the question of Indian protection comes up at all. That earlier registration is both an asset and, depending on the route chosen, a liability for the Indian filing, because the two main ways of reaching the Indian register treat the home registration very differently.

The first route is to designate India within an international application or an existing international registration filed through the World Intellectual Property Organization under the Madrid Protocol, using the applicant's home registration or application as the basic mark the international filing builds on. The second route is to instruct an Indian trademark agent or attorney to file a fresh national application directly before the Trade Marks Registry, treating the Indian filing as a free-standing application that happens to belong to a company that also owns marks elsewhere.

Both routes end in the same place, a trademark on the Indian register enforceable under the same Trade Marks Act, 1999 as any mark owned by an Indian company. They differ sharply, however, in how the registration is obtained, how long it takes, how exposed it stays to events in the applicant's home country, and how much room there is to adjust the specification of goods or services for how Indian examiners and later Indian courts actually read it.

The choice is also not strictly binary in practice. A foreign group with a broad international portfolio sometimes designates India for most of its marks through Madrid while filing a handful of its more commercially sensitive or more recently launched marks directly, precisely to keep those specific filings free of the home mark's dependency risk. Nothing in the Act or the Protocol requires a single company to pick one route and use it for every mark; the decision can, and often should, be made mark by mark rather than once for the whole portfolio.

sections.heading: India's Accession and the Chapter Built to Receive It
paragraphs: India deposited its instrument of accession to the Madrid Protocol with the World Intellectual Property Organization on 8 April 2013, becoming the 90th member of the Madrid Union, and the Protocol entered into force for India three months later, on 8 July 2013. Before that date, a foreign company had only the direct filing route available in India, regardless of how many other Madrid members it already held registrations in.

The domestic mechanism for receiving Madrid designations was put in place by the Trade Marks (Amendment) Act, 2010, Act No. 40 of 2010, which inserted a new Chapter IVA into the Trade Marks Act, 1999 specifically to apply to international applications and international registrations under the Madrid Protocol. The Amendment Act had been passed in 2010, well before India's actual accession, and was itself brought into force, together with the corresponding Trade Marks (Amendment) Rules, 2013, by a notification effective from 8 July 2013, the same date the Protocol itself took effect for India, so that the domestic legal machinery and India's international treaty obligation began operating on the same day.

The gap between 2010, when the Amendment Act inserting Chapter IVA was passed, and 2013, when it actually took effect alongside India's accession, explains why some older Indian trademark commentary discusses the Madrid Protocol only in the future tense. India signalled its intention to join the Madrid system well before the domestic machinery and the treaty accession itself were both actually in place, and any source discussing Indian trademark practice from before July 2013 should be read as describing the direct-filing-only era rather than the current, dual-route position.

A foreign company's Indian counsel confirming that a particular international registration validly covers India should be looking at this Chapter IVA framework specifically, rather than at the ordinary Chapter III and IV provisions that govern a direct national application, since the two chapters, though they converge on the same register, run on separate procedural tracks within the Act for matters such as the timing of refusal and the recording of subsequent changes.

This also explains why an Indian trademark search of the register alone does not always tell a foreign company everything it needs to know about a competing mark's status in India. A Madrid designation that is still within its examination window, or that has not yet been advertised, may not show up in an ordinary register search the way a direct application does once filed, so a foreign company conducting clearance before launching a brand in India should specifically ask its search provider to check WIPO's own Madrid Monitor data for pending designations of India, alongside the Indian Registry's own published records rather than instead of them.

sections.heading: How a Madrid Designation of India Actually Proceeds
paragraphs: Once the International Bureau at WIPO notifies India of a designation, the Indian Trade Marks Registry examines it broadly the way it would examine a direct application, checking for conflicts with earlier marks and for the absolute grounds of refusal under Section 9, principally descriptiveness, lack of distinctiveness and marks that are deceptive or scandalous, and the relative grounds under Section 11, principally conflict with an existing registered or well-known mark. Where the Registry finds no obstacle and no opposition is filed within the statutory window, the mark proceeds to protection in India without the applicant or its Indian counsel ever having filed a free-standing Indian application form.

Where the Registry does find an obstacle, it issues what the Madrid system calls a provisional refusal, communicated to WIPO and from there to the applicant or its representative, and the applicant then has to respond substantively, often by engaging Indian counsel for the first time at that point even though the designation itself required no Indian filing to begin with. This is one of the more common surprises for a foreign company that assumed the Madrid route meant it would never need Indian representation at all; it usually does, just later in the process than under a direct filing.

A designation that survives examination and any opposition without a provisional refusal being notified within the window India has declared is treated as protected in India from the date of the international registration, or from the date of any later designation of India, as if it had proceeded to registration under the ordinary Act, and from that point it is enforceable in Indian courts in the same way as any other Indian trademark registration.

A foreign applicant does not need to appoint an Indian agent merely to file the designation itself, since that step happens entirely through WIPO and the applicant's home office. It is only when the Registry raises a provisional refusal, or when a third party opposes, that Indian representation actually becomes necessary, and a foreign company that treats the absence of an early requirement for Indian counsel as a sign the matter needs no attention at all risks missing the response deadline once a provisional refusal does arrive, since that deadline runs from the date of the refusal, not from whenever the company happens to notice it in its own inbox.

sections.heading: The 18-Month Window and What Silence Actually Means
paragraphs: Under Article 5(2) of the Madrid Protocol, a member country can choose to extend the standard one-year period for notifying a provisional refusal to 18 months, and India made that declaration, so a foreign company designating India should plan for an examination and opposition period that can run considerably longer than the equivalent window in a Madrid member that kept the shorter default period.

The 18-month figure is not simply a courtesy extension for the Registry's own convenience. India's declaration specifically carries the extended period under Article 5(2)(c) for a refusal that results from an opposition, which means even a mark that cleared substantive examination within a shorter window can still be hit with a provisional refusal arising from a third party's opposition at any point up to the full 18 months, and a foreign company should not treat early silence from the Registry as a final answer before that window has actually run.

If no provisional refusal is notified within the applicable window, the designation is treated as protected in India, and the practical lesson for a foreign brand owner is less about the law and more about internal process: someone on the trademark team, whether in-house or at the instructing firm, has to actually track the 18-month date for each Indian designation rather than assume that an absence of correspondence after the first year means the matter is closed.

sections.heading: Central Attack: Why the Home Mark's Health Still Matters
paragraphs: The feature of the Madrid system that most distinguishes it from a direct filing, and the one a foreign company's Indian counsel should flag before any designation is made, is the international registration's dependency on the basic mark for the first five years from the date of international registration. If the basic mark, the application or registration in the applicant's home office that the international registration was built on, is successfully challenged, refused, withdrawn, or otherwise ceases to have effect within that five-year window, every designation built on it, India included, falls with it. This is generally known as central attack, and it is the price paid for the convenience of a single, centrally filed application covering multiple countries.

The five-year clock runs from the international registration date, not from the date India specifically was designated, and not from the date Indian protection actually took effect after examination, which means a foreign company can find its Indian protection unwound by a dispute over the home mark that has nothing to do with India and that Indian counsel may not even be tracking unless specifically asked to.

A proceeding against the basic mark that begins before the five-year window closes can still result in cancellation of the international registration, and everything built on it, even if the final decision in that proceeding is handed down after the five years have technically run. A foreign company should treat the home mark as live exposure for the full five years, not merely for the nominal duration of the window itself, and should keep its Indian counsel informed of any opposition, cancellation or invalidity proceeding against the home registration the moment it is filed, rather than only after it is decided.

sections.heading: What a Madrid Designation Still Does Not Do Easily in India
paragraphs: Beyond the central attack risk, practitioners who handle both routes into India point to a narrower set of practical frictions specific to the Madrid designation. Historically, the Indian Registry has been slower to accept a disclaimer or a limitation on a Madrid-designated application than on a directly filed one, a gap that commentary flagged some years ago and that a foreign company should specifically ask its Indian counsel to confirm against current Registry practice before assuming either that the restriction still applies or that it has been resolved, since this is exactly the kind of procedural detail that changes without always being well publicised.

A related friction concerns the specification of goods and services itself. Many foreign basic applications are filed with broad, standard-form descriptions acceptable in the applicant's home office, and Indian examiners do not always accept the same breadth, sometimes requiring the specification to be narrowed to be allowed in India specifically. A direct filing gives the applicant's Indian counsel the chance to draft the specification with Indian classification practice in mind from the outset; a Madrid designation generally carries over the international registration's specification and then has to be narrowed, if at all, through the examination correspondence after a provisional refusal, which is a slower and less controlled way of arriving at the same result.

sections.heading: Filing Directly in India: What a Foreign Applicant Actually Needs
paragraphs: A foreign company that files directly in India, whether because it has no convenient home basic mark, because the home mark is itself contested, or because it simply wants India handled as its own matter from the outset, needs an address for service in India on the application, which in practice is almost always the office address of the Indian trademark attorney or agent instructed for the filing, together with a postal and an email address the Registry can use for all subsequent correspondence. Without a valid address for service, the Registry is not obliged to issue notices to the applicant directly, and an order made in the meantime cannot later be challenged for want of notice.

Because the foreign applicant cannot appear in person before the Registry, it authorises its Indian attorney to act through a power of attorney on Form TM-48, which functions as the binding authorisation the Registry requires before it will accept any filing or response from that attorney on the applicant's behalf. Where the power of attorney is executed outside India, Indian trademark agents generally insist on it being notarised and, depending on the country of execution, apostilled or otherwise legalised, before relying on it for an Indian filing, and building this execution step into the company's own signing and courier timeline, rather than leaving it until a deadline is close, avoids a surprisingly common cause of delay in an otherwise straightforward direct filing.

Unlike the Madrid route, a direct filing does not require any underlying home registration or application at all. A foreign company launching a genuinely new brand that has not yet been registered anywhere can file directly in India on that basis alone, provided it otherwise satisfies the ordinary requirements of the Act, which is not something the Madrid route can offer, since a Madrid designation necessarily depends on a basic mark already on file somewhere.

A direct application also lets the applicant file across multiple classes of goods or services in a single application, which India permits, rather than being limited to the classes the basic mark happened to cover at home. A foreign company whose Indian business plan already extends beyond the categories its home registration protects, a packaged goods brand planning to add a retail or a food-service offering in India, for instance, often finds it cleaner to capture the fuller Indian scope in one direct filing than to layer a second Madrid designation, or a separate direct application, on top of an existing designation later.

sections.heading: Claiming an Earlier Priority Date Under Section 154
paragraphs: A direct filing need not start its priority clock from the Indian filing date alone. Section 154 of the Trade Marks Act, 1999 lets an applicant who has already applied for registration of the same mark in a convention country claim the benefit of that earlier filing date, provided the Indian application is made within six months of the earlier filing. Where the earlier mark was filed in more than one convention country, the six months runs from the earliest of those filings, not from whichever one the applicant finds most convenient to rely on.

This priority claim is made on Form TM-2 and generally needs to be supported by a certificate from the foreign trademarks office confirming the particulars of the earlier filing, in line with the requirement under the Trade Marks Rules that the Indian application state the filing date of the convention application; where the earlier application's own number is not yet known at the time of the Indian filing, practice allows it to be supplied within two months of the Indian filing date instead of holding up the filing itself. Missing the six-month window is generally treated as fatal to the priority claim specifically, not to the Indian application as a whole; the Indian filing still proceeds, but it proceeds from its own actual filing date rather than the earlier, more favourable one, which can matter considerably if a third party filed a conflicting mark in the gap between the two dates.

A foreign company planning a near-simultaneous global launch should calendar this six-month window the moment the first application is filed anywhere in a convention country, since it is the Indian filing date that has to fall inside the window, not merely the decision to file in India, and six months passes considerably faster during a product launch than most marketing timelines account for.

sections.heading: Examination, Opposition and the Four Months That Cannot Be Extended
paragraphs: Whichever route brings a mark onto the Indian register, once it clears substantive examination it is advertised in the Trade Marks Journal, and any person at all, with or without a registered right of its own, can file a notice of opposition under Section 21(1) within four months of that advertisement or re-advertisement. The current wording of Section 21(1) does not allow this period to be extended, a deliberate tightening from the earlier regime, which had allowed a shorter base period together with a further extension of up to a month.

Once an opposition is filed, the applicant has two months from receiving the notice to file a counter-statement under Section 21(2), and failing to do so within that period is generally treated as abandoning the application so far as that opposition is concerned. For a foreign applicant managing its Indian filing from outside the country, often through an Indian agent who in turn reports to in-house counsel or an international firm managing the global trademark portfolio, the four-month opposition window and the two-month counter-statement window are the two dates in the entire Indian process most likely to be missed through nothing more than a chain of email forwards taking slightly too long, and both deserve their own calendared reminder independent of whatever docketing system tracks the matter generally.

A Madrid designation runs through the same Section 21 opposition mechanism once it is advertised, so the same four-month, non-extendable clock applies to it as to a direct filing; the Madrid route changes how the application reaches advertisement, not what happens to it once it gets there.

sections.heading: Well-Known Mark Status: A Separate, Optional Layer of Protection
paragraphs: Independent of the registration route chosen, a foreign company with genuine, provable reputation in India, even without an Indian registration yet in force, can seek recognition of its mark as a well-known trade mark under Section 2(1)(zg) read with Section 11(6) of the Act, which extends protection against a conflicting mark across classes of goods or services the well-known mark may not itself be registered for. This is a meaningfully broader form of protection than an ordinary registration, which generally protects only within the classes actually registered.

The Registry's own procedure for recognising a mark as well-known runs under Rule 124 of the Trade Marks Rules, 2017, on an application in Form TM-M supported by evidence of the mark's reputation among the relevant public, and is reported to carry a separate fee in the region of Rs 1,00,000, a materially higher figure than an ordinary application fee, reflecting that this is a discretionary, evidence-heavy declaration rather than a routine filing. The Registry has indicated that it does not itself adjudicate the underlying question of whether a mark is well known in a contested sense; its role under Rule 124 is to process the application and, where satisfied on the material placed before it, include the mark in the list of well-known marks it maintains.

A mark can also come to be treated as well known through a court's or the Registrar's own finding during the trial of some other proceeding, such as an infringement suit, rather than through a standalone Rule 124 application, and there is genuine, unresolved debate in the commentary and before the courts over whether a mark recognised that way still needs to go through the Rule 124 procedure and fee to be formally listed, or whether the court's or Registrar's finding is itself sufficient. A foreign company that already has a reputation-based finding in its favour from Indian litigation should get specific advice on whether a separate Rule 124 listing is worth pursuing, rather than assume the point is settled either way.

sections.heading: Keeping the Registration Alive: Renewal, Restoration and Non-Use
paragraphs: An Indian trademark registration, however it was obtained, lasts ten years from the date of registration and can be renewed indefinitely, but the renewal mechanics run on a stricter clock than many foreign applicants expect. Under Section 25(2) read with Rule 57(1) of the Trade Marks Rules, 2017, the in-time renewal application can be filed at any point within one year before the registration's expiry; a foreign company used to a shorter standard renewal window elsewhere should not assume Indian practice mirrors it.

Missing that window is not immediately fatal. The proviso to Section 25(3), read with Rule 59, allows a late renewal within six months after expiry on payment of the prescribed fee together with a surcharge, and the surcharge actually has to be paid for this route to apply; a filing that omits it has been held not to engage the proviso at all, leaving the Registrar to remove the mark from the register. Beyond that six-month late-renewal window, but within one year of the original expiry date, Section 25(4) allows restoration of an already-removed mark on Form TM-R, on payment of a higher restoration fee than either the ordinary or the late renewal fee.

Once twelve months have passed from the original expiry date without renewal or restoration, the mark is ordinarily struck off the register for good, and a foreign company that wants to use the same mark in India again generally has to file an entirely fresh application, competing for priority against anything filed in the interim, with none of the earlier registration's priority or seniority carried forward. For a foreign company managing a large global portfolio through an external renewal-tracking service, it is worth specifically confirming that the service's calendar for the Indian entries runs on this one-year-before, six-months-after, twelve-months-final sequence rather than on whatever generic renewal window the service applies to jurisdictions elsewhere.

A registration already five years old, counted from its date of registration, carries a separate exposure as well: a rectification petition under Section 47(1)(b) on the ground of non-use, where the mark has not actually been used in India for a continuous period of five years, measured up to three months before the rectification petition is filed, and a competitor or any other aggrieved person can apply to have it removed on that basis. Section 47(3) offers a defence where the non-use is due to special circumstances in the trade, such as a genuine, documented restriction on importing or dealing in the relevant goods, but the defence is understood to be lost where the non-use instead reflects an intention to abandon the mark, so a foreign company holding an Indian registration purely defensively, with no present plan to trade under it in India, should weigh that exposure against the cost of maintaining some minimal, genuine use.

sections.heading: Choosing the Route That Actually Suits the Company
paragraphs: For a foreign company that already holds registrations across a wide spread of Madrid member countries and has a stable, unchallenged home basic mark, designating India alongside the rest of that portfolio is usually the more efficient route, since it avoids instructing separate Indian counsel for the initial filing and keeps the renewal date aligned with the rest of the international registration.

For a company whose Indian interest is more or less a standalone matter, where India is one of only a handful of markets the brand actually trades in, where the home basic mark is itself newly filed, contested, or otherwise less than fully secure, or where the specification needs meaningful tailoring to Indian classification practice from the outset, a direct filing generally gives more control for a cost difference that is usually smaller than the central attack risk and the specification friction are worth. A company in genuine doubt about which category it falls into is better served asking its Indian counsel to model both routes against its specific facts than choosing on the strength of a general preference either way.

sections.heading: A Practical Filing Sequence for a First Indian Filing
paragraphs: The first step is deciding the route itself, weighing the health and stability of the home basic mark, the breadth of the company's existing Madrid portfolio, and how far the standard specification will need to be narrowed for India, before instructing anyone to file anything.

The second step, for a direct filing, is executing the Form TM-48 power of attorney in favour of Indian counsel early enough to allow for notarisation and apostille from the country of execution, and confirming the address for service that will appear on the application, since correcting either after filing is more cumbersome than getting them right at the outset.

The third step, where an earlier convention filing exists and the Indian filing can still be made within six months of it, is claiming priority under Section 154 on Form TM-2 rather than defaulting to the Indian filing date, and chasing down the foreign office's filing certificate promptly enough to meet the two-month window for supplying the application number if it was not available when the Indian filing was made.

The fourth step, for either route, is calendaring the 18-month Madrid window or the ordinary examination timeline, the four-month opposition window once advertisement happens, and, once registered, the one-year-before and six-months-after renewal dates, as distinct entries in whatever docketing system the company's trademark function already uses, rather than relying on a general reminder that a given jurisdiction's registration exists and needs attention at some unspecified point.

sections.heading: What Remains Unsettled
paragraphs: Two practical points deserve a specific check against current practice rather than reliance on this piece alone. Whether the Indian Registry still declines to accept a disclaimer or limitation on a Madrid-designated application in the way older commentary described has not been confirmed here against a current Registry circular or a recent, reported instance either way, and a foreign company for whom this specifically matters should have its Indian counsel test the point against the Registry's present practice before relying on either answer. Separately, the debate over whether a mark recognised as well known by a court's finding during litigation, rather than through a standalone Rule 124 application, still needs a formal Rule 124 listing and fee to receive the full practical benefit of that status has not been resolved by a reported decision this piece can point to with confidence, and a foreign company holding such a finding should treat the listing question as open rather than settled in either direction.

conclusion: Neither route into the Indian trademark register is free of its own friction, and the right choice depends on facts specific to the company rather than a general rule that favours one over the other. A Madrid designation buys convenience and portfolio-wide alignment at the cost of five years of dependency on a mark the company may be managing, and defending, in an entirely different legal system. A direct filing buys independence and more control over the specification at the cost of a separate filing, a separate power of attorney, and a separate set of dates to track from the outset. Working out which trade-off actually suits the company's position, before the first application is filed rather than after a provisional refusal or an opposition forces the question, is the one step in this entire process that genuinely cannot be delegated to a form.

faqs.q: Can a foreign company file a trademark application in India without any registration at home?
faqs.a: Yes, through a direct national filing. The Madrid Protocol route specifically requires an existing basic mark at home or in another office, but a direct filing before the Indian Trade Marks Registry does not.

faqs.q: What is central attack, and why does it matter for a Madrid designation of India?
faqs.a: An international registration depends on its basic mark for five years from the international registration date. If that basic mark is successfully challenged or cancelled within that period, every designation built on it, including India, falls with it, which is a risk a direct Indian filing does not carry.

faqs.q: How long does India take to raise an objection to a Madrid-designated application?
faqs.a: India has declared an 18-month period under the Madrid Protocol for notifying a provisional refusal, including one arising from an opposition, rather than the shorter default period some other member countries use.

faqs.q: Can a foreign applicant claim an earlier priority date for an Indian filing?
faqs.a: Yes, under Section 154 of the Trade Marks Act, 1999, provided the Indian application is filed within six months of an earlier application for the same mark in a convention country, with the clock running from the earliest such filing if there is more than one.

faqs.q: How long does a foreign applicant have to oppose, or respond to an opposition against, an Indian trademark application?
faqs.a: A notice of opposition must be filed within four months of advertisement under Section 21(1), a period that cannot currently be extended, and the applicant then has two months from receiving that notice to file a counter-statement under Section 21(2).

faqs.q: What happens if an Indian trademark registration is not renewed on time?
faqs.a: A late renewal is possible within six months of expiry on payment of a surcharge under the proviso to Section 25(3). Beyond that, restoration remains possible up to one year after expiry at a higher fee under Section 25(4). After twelve months, the mark is generally struck off for good and has to be refiled afresh.

faqs.q: Can an Indian trademark registration be cancelled for non-use?
faqs.a: Yes, under Section 47(1)(b), where the mark has not been used in India for a continuous period of five years, counted up to three months before a rectification petition is filed, subject to a defence under Section 47(3) for genuine special circumstances in the trade.

faqs.q: Does well-known mark status in India require a separate application?
faqs.a: Usually yes, through Form TM-M under Rule 124 of the Trade Marks Rules, 2017, supported by evidence of reputation and a separate fee. A mark can also be found well known by a court or the Registrar during other proceedings, though whether that finding alone dispenses with a formal Rule 124 listing is not yet settled.
